deepDive.title: Trophic levels and food pyramids — energy flow through ecosystems
deepDive.body: Class 7 introduces food chains. Class 8 stacks them into TROPHIC LEVELS — energy hierarchy. Level 1: PRODUCERS (plants, ~100% of sun's energy captured). Level 2: PRIMARY CONSUMERS (herbivores — deer, rabbits, grasshoppers). Level 3: SECONDARY CONSUMERS (carnivores eating herbivores — frogs, snakes). Level 4: TERTIARY CONSUMERS (top carnivores — tigers, eagles). 10% RULE: only ~10% of energy passes from one level to the next; 90% lost as heat / used by the organism. So 10,000 kg of grass → 1000 kg of deer → 100 kg of leopard → 10 kg of tiger. That's why top predators are rare — there's just not enough energy to support many of them. India's Western Ghats can support only ~50 tigers per 1000 sq km — the ecosystem's energy ceiling.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle after Class 7 food chain basics.
deepDive.nextStepHint: Class 11 introduces gross vs net primary productivity calculations.

deepDive.title: Ecological niche, succession, and biodiversity
deepDive.body: Class 7 describes forest layers and animals. Class 11 introduces ECOLOGICAL NICHE — the specific 'job' each species does in its ecosystem (food, shelter, role). Two species can't have identical niches — one outcompetes (Gause's principle). Indian tiger vs leopard: niche overlap, but leopard is smaller, climbs trees (different prey size, different microhabitat). SUCCESSION: how ecosystems change over time. PRIMARY SUCCESSION: bare rock → lichens → mosses → grasses → shrubs → trees (centuries to millennia). SECONDARY SUCCESSION: after disturbance (fire, clearing), faster (decades). BIODIVERSITY: species count + ecological diversity + genetic diversity. Western Ghats has high biodiversity (5000+ plant species, 1700 endemic). Higher biodiversity = more resilient ecosystem.
deepDive.nextStepHint: Class 12 covers in-situ vs ex-situ conservation and IUCN Red List criteria.

deepDive.title: Decomposer chemistry — what happens at molecular level
deepDive.body: Class 7 says decomposers break down dead matter. Class 10 names the chemistry. Major nutrients cycle: NITROGEN — dead organisms' proteins → bacteria break to amino acids → AMMONIFYING bacteria release ammonia (NH₃) → NITRIFYING bacteria oxidise to nitrate (NO₃⁻) → roots absorb. CARBON — dead matter's carbohydrates → fungi + bacteria break to CO₂ + small molecules → CO₂ enters atmosphere → photosynthesis pulls back. PHOSPHORUS — dead organisms' DNA + bone → bacteria release phosphate → roots absorb. Each cycle takes weeks (carbon) to centuries (phosphorus). Earthworms, dung beetles, fungi, bacteria — all play roles. Disrupting any one (e.g., by overusing chemical fungicides) breaks the chain. Forest soil's amazing fertility comes from decomposer chemistry running continuously, free.
